newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela offers 35 percent pay rise to unions.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela offers 35 percent pay rise to unions.

text.p: After nearly two months of strikes and strident public debate, the Venezuelan government has reached a pre-accord with public sector workers offering them a 35 percent pay rise for 1997, Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar said.
"Our proposal is a 35 percent salary increase, above expected inflation of 25 percent, as well a 50 percent increase in monthly bonuses," Matos said during a presentation to Congress.
Although Matos said "labor are asking for a 125 percent increase," he said he hoped agreement would be reached in the next few days.

The new proposal, which tops earlier government offers of a 25 percent rise, was signed this morning with Venezuela's largest public sector union, the Confederation of Venezuelan Workers (CTV). However, it still has to be cleared with other Venezuelan unions.
Finance Ministry officials told Reuters the offer is on a sliding scale that would boost minimum public sector take home pay to 90,000 bolivars a month from current levels of 53,000.

Much of the rise comes from a monthly bonus of 26,000 bolivars which Matos said could be converted into salary if ongoing tripartite talks with union and private sector leaders over social security reforms were successful.

In January, the government awarded an average 164 percent pay rise to striking doctors, fanning other wage demands. Analysts have feared further high public sector wage increases could burst Venezuela's budget and send inflation soaring.
But Matos told reporters earlier Wednesday: "No one can expect this government to put right in one stroke the problem of Venezuela's low real wages, which has accumulated over the past 15 years."
Venezuelan real wages, laid waste by triple digit inflation last year, have shrunk to some 30 percent of 1980 levels, according to government estimates.
